analysis.one_liner: Repeals FISA and requires warrants before the government can surveil Americans.
analysis.headline: Rep. Andy Biggs' bill to repeal the FISA surveillance law and require court warrants to spy on Americans was introduced with zero cosponsors and has sat in two House committees with no action since January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), the 1978 law that sets the rules for government spying in foreign-intelligence cases. In its place, it would require federal agents to get a normal criminal-court warrant before wiretapping, searching, or targeting any U.S. citizen, and it would ban using information about citizens gathered under executive-branch rules or picked up during surveillance of foreigners in any court case or investigation. Government officials who spy on Americans without a warrant, or knowingly use such tainted information, could be fined up to $10,000 and imprisoned for at least five years.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans would gain: their phone calls, emails, homes, and records could not be monitored without a judge's warrant under standard criminal-court rules, no matter whether the government says the purpose is foreign intelligence. Evidence about a citizen collected under Executive Order 12333 or swept up while watching a foreigner could no longer be used against that citizen in any criminal, civil, or administrative proceeding. The criminal penalty gives citizens a way to hold officials personally accountable if those lines are crossed.

how_it_helps.text: Requires any U.S. government officer to obtain a warrant from a federal court under ordinary criminal procedures before conducting electronic surveillance, a physical search, a pen register or trap-and-trace order, or a records demand targeting a U.S. citizen, or before targeting a citizen for foreign-intelligence collection.

Bars the use of information about a U.S. citizen gathered under Executive Order 12333, or acquired while surveilling a non-citizen, against that citizen in any criminal, civil, or administrative proceeding or investigation — closing the path by which foreign-intelligence data has historically reached domestic cases.

Creates criminal liability — a fine of up to $10,000, imprisonment of not less than five years, or both — for officials who intentionally surveil citizens without a warrant or who knowingly disclose or use information obtained that way, with a defense only for conduct authorized by a search warrant or court order.

analysis.who_pays: The intelligence community and federal law enforcement would bear the cost: repealing FISA would eliminate the entire court-approved framework for foreign-intelligence surveillance, not just the parts that touch Americans, and officials would face prison time for warrantless surveillance of citizens. National security agencies contend that stripped-down authorities would shrink their ability to track foreign spies and terrorists.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals all of FISA, not just the provisions affecting Americans — eliminating the court-approval process for spying on foreign agents, terrorists, and hostile governments entirely, rather than fixing only the part where Americans get swept in.

The blanket ban on using any information about a citizen gathered under Executive Order 12333 or picked up incidentally during surveillance of a foreigner could block prosecutors from using real evidence in genuine cases, including evidence of serious crimes discovered in foreign-intelligence collection.

The penalty structure is blunt: any intentional violation carries at least five years in prison, while the fine is capped at just $10,000 — a lopsided mandatory sentence that could chill legitimate intelligence work done in good faith near the line.

The protections cover only U.S. citizens. Green-card holders and other non-citizens living in the United States would not get the same warrant shield, leaving a large group of residents outside the bill's protection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — that Americans should not have their communications and records collected without a judge's warrant — addresses a real and long-running grievance. But the bill is a sledgehammer: full repeal of FISA removes all court oversight of foreign spying, the use-bans could tie prosecutors' hands in legitimate cases, the mandatory five-year minimum is blunt, and non-citizens in the U.S. get nothing. A narrower bill aimed at surveillance of Americans could have delivered most of the privacy gain with far less counterintelligence risk.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary and Intelligence committees, and with no cosponsors and no hearings or votes scheduled, it has simply sat there for the rest of the session so far.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs introduced the bill on January 3, 2025, the first day of the new Congress.

The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the Intelligence Committee, with the Speaker to decide later how to split jurisdiction — a routine step for bills touching two areas.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor, and no committee hearing, markup, or floor vote has occurred since referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The intelligence and law enforcement agencies are better off: the current FISA framework, with its streamlined foreign-surveillance authorities, remains in force untouched. Americans' surveillance rights are exactly where they were before the bill was filed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Intelligence agencies; current surveillance powers continue

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 119th Congress and referred it to two committees; recruited no cosponsors

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever took place and no other member from either party cosponsored the bill, so there is no recorded partisan split — the only documented support is the single Republican sponsor.

industries.industry: Intelligence and law enforcement agencies (FBI, NSA, CIA)
industries.note: These agencies would lose FISA's court-approved foreign-surveillance framework and face five-year prison terms for warrantless surveillance of citizens, so their institutional interest runs directly against the bill. Their counterargument — that the same tools catch foreign spies and terrorists — is the price ordinary people would pay for the privacy gain.

Phone and internet providers currently receive FISA orders compelling them to hand over customer data. Repealing FISA would end that compelled-assistance regime but also erase the statutory framework that defines providers' obligations and legal cover, leaving the rules for cooperation with surveillance uncertain.

analysis.trajectory: Congress is still in session, so the bill is technically alive, but with zero cosponsors and no movement in either committee since January 2025, it is likely to sit until the session ends without ever getting a hearing or a vote — the usual fate of single-sponsor surveillance-overhaul bills.
